l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Mencius, occupying the position of a high dignitary in Qi, went on a mission of condolence to Teng. He did not discuss the business of the mission with Wang Huan because proper officers attended to it.

l: Wang Huan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Wang Huan, the governor of Gai, was sent by the king as assistant-commissioner. He waited upon Mencius morning and evening during the journey to Teng and back.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Qi was the place where Mencius held the position of a high dignitary. Its king sent Wang Huan as assistant-commissioner on the mission to Teng.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Teng was the destination of Mencius's mission of condolence from Qi.

l: mission of condolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The mission of condolence went from Qi to Teng and back. Its business was attended to by proper officers rather than discussed between Mencius and Wang Huan.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius traveled from Qi to Lu to bury his mother and stopped at Ying on his return to Qi. Chong Yu questioned Mencius about the quality of the coffin used for his mother, saying that the wood seemed too good. Mencius explained that traditional coffin thickness applied to everyone and fulfilled natural feelings, including the desire to protect the bodies of the dead from the earth. He concluded that a superior man is not niggardly toward his parents.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius went from Qi to Lu to bury his mother and stopped at Ying while returning to Qi. He defended using good wood for the coffin, saying that traditional practices satisfied natural feelings and that a superior man is not niggardly toward his parents.

l: Chong Yu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Chong Yu begged to question Mencius at Ying. He asked about the coffin because he thought its wood was too good.

l: mother (Mencius's mother), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius's mother was buried in Lu by Mencius.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius traveled from Qi to Lu and returned toward Qi after burying his mother.

l: coffin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: The coffin used for Mencius's mother was made with wood that Chong Yu considered too good. Mencius said that coffins had traditionally been made thick enough to satisfy natural feelings and protect the dead from the earth.

l: burial of Mencius's mother, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius went from Qi to Lu to bury his mother, then returned toward Qi.

l: making of the coffin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Chong Yu had been employed to superintend the making of the coffin. Mencius explained that ancient practice used substantial coffin construction for everyone, from the sovereign to common people.

l: conversation about the coffin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: At Ying, Chong Yu questioned Mencius about the quality of the coffin. Mencius defended the choice by appealing to traditional practice and natural feelings toward one's parents.

l: natural feelings, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius said that traditional coffin construction satisfied people's natural feelings. He also identified satisfaction in preventing the earth from getting near the bodies of the dead.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Shen Tong asked Mencius whether Yan might be smitten. Mencius said that it might because Zi Kuai had no right to give Yan away and Zi Zhi had no right to receive it. The people of Qi then smote Yan, and Mencius denied that he had advised Qi to do so. He explained that he would have said only that the minister of Heaven could smite Yan, not that Qi could do it.

l: Shen Tong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Shen Tong asked Mencius whether Yan might be smitten. He did so on his own impulse, without the text saying that he asked who might smite it.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Mencius said that Yan might be smitten because Zi Kuai had no right to give it to another man and Zi Zhi had no right to receive it. He denied advising Qi to smite Yan, explaining that he had answered only the question of whether it might be smitten.

l: Zi Kuai, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Zi Kuai had no right to give Yan to another man.

l: Zi Zhi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Zi Zhi had no right to receive Yan from Zi Kuai.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Qi smote Yan, but Mencius said he had not advised Qi to do so. Mencius stated that the minister of Heaven, rather than Qi as such, could smite Yan.

l: the people of Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: The people of Qi smote Yan after Shen Tong asked Mencius whether Yan might be smitten.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Yan was treated by Mencius as a case in which Zi Kuai had no right to give it away and Zi Zhi had no right to receive it. The people of Qi smote Yan, which Mencius questioned by asking how one Yan could smite another Yan.

l: the smiting of Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: The smiting of Yan followed Mencius's statement that Yan might be smitten. Mencius clarified that he would have authorized it only if carried out by the minister of Heaven, not by Qi.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: The people of Yan rebelled, causing the king of Qi to feel ashamed when he thought of Mencius. Chen Jia compared the king with Zhou Gong and argued that even Zhou Gong had lacked benevolence or knowledge if he knowingly or unknowingly appointed Guan Shu, who later rebelled with the Yin State. Mencius explained that Zhou Gong did not know Guan Shu would rebel and that his appointment of his elder brother was understandable. Mencius said that superior men of old reformed their errors, while those of the present persist in errors and apologize for them.

l: people of Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: The people of Yan rebelled.

l: king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: The king of Qi felt very much ashamed when he thought of Mencius. Chen Jia sought to relieve him from that feeling by comparing him with Zhou Gong.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius said that Zhou Gong was an ancient sage and did not know Guan Shu would rebel. He taught that superior men of old reformed their errors, whereas superior men of the present persist in them and apologize for them.

l: Chen Jia, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Chen Jia told the king of Qi not to grieve and compared the king's benevolence and wisdom with those of Zhou Gong. He then saw Mencius and questioned him about Zhou Gong and Guan Shu.

l: duke of Zhou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Zhou Gong appointed Guan Shu to oversee the heir of Yin without knowing that Guan Shu would rebel. Mencius said that, because Guan Shu was Zhou Gong's elder brother, the appointment was in accordance with what was right.

l: Guan Shu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Guan Shu was appointed by Zhou Gong to oversee the heir of Yin. He used the power of the Yin State to rebel.

l: Yin dynasty, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Guan Shu used the power of the Yin State to rebel.

l: rebellion of the people of Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: The rebellion of the people of Yan led the king of Qi to feel ashamed when he thought of Mencius.

l: rebellion of Guan Shu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Guan Shu rebelled with the power of the Yin State after being appointed to oversee the heir of Yin.

l: appointment of Guan Shu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Zhou Gong appointed Guan Shu to oversee the heir of Yin. Mencius said Zhou Gong did not know that Guan Shu would rebel and that the appointment was understandable because Guan Shu was his elder brother.

l: error, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius said that Zhou Gong's error was in accordance with what was right. He contrasted the errors of superior men of old, which they reformed, with those of present superior men, who persist in them and apologize for them.

l: reformation of errors, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Superior men of old reformed their errors. After reforming, they were again regarded by the people with their former admiration.

l: shame of the king of Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: The king of Qi experienced shame when he thought of Mencius because the people of Yan had rebelled.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius gave up his office and arranged to return to his native State. The king visited him, expressed regret at his departure, and said he did not know whether he would see Mencius again. The king later proposed giving Mencius a house and supporting his disciples with an allowance of 10,000 zhong. Mencius declined, explaining that accepting the offer would appear inconsistent with his rejection of 100,000 zhong and his lack of desire for riches.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius gave up his office and arranged to return to his native State. He said that he desired to visit the king, though he did not request permission to do so at a particular time. He declined the king's proposed house and allowance, saying that accepting 10,000 zhong would not be the conduct of one desiring riches.

l: the king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: The king visited Mencius and expressed regret that Mencius was leaving, saying that he did not know whether he would have another opportunity to see him. He later proposed giving Mencius a house in the middle of the kingdom and supporting his disciples with 10,000 zhong.

l: officer Shi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: The officer Shi was told by the king to convey the proposal about a house and an allowance to Mencius. He conveyed the message through the disciple Chen.

l: native State, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius arranged to return to his native State after giving up his office.

l: office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius gave up his office and made arrangements to return to his native State.

l: riches and honour, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius said that people generally desire riches and honour, but he denied that his conduct showed a desire for riches. He referred to a man who tried to monopolize the conspicuous mound in the market as an example of mean conduct motivated by gain.

l: the king's visit to Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: The king's visit gave him an opportunity to be by Mencius's side, which made his court rejoice. During the visit, the king expressed concern that Mencius was leaving and might not be seen again.

l: Mencius's departure from office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius's departure from office led him to make arrangements to return to his native State. The king regretted this departure and later considered offering Mencius a house and support for his disciples.

l: Mencius's return home, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius arranged to return home after giving up his office. He said that he desired to visit the king, although he did not request permission to do so at a particular time.

l: taxing of traders, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 10
s: The taxing of traders was said to have begun because a mean fellow sought a conspicuous mound in the market to look over the traders and capture the whole gain. The people regarded his conduct as mean and proceeded to lay a tax on the traders' wares.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: Mencius, having left Qi, spent the night in Zhou. A visitor who wished to detain him on behalf of the king approached him, but Mencius gave no answer and slept. Mencius explained that the duke Mou had retained Zi Si through proper treatment and said that the visitor's plans did not treat him similarly.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: Mencius left Qi and spent the night in Zhou. He ignored a visitor's initial speech by sleeping, then explained that he was not being treated as Zi Si had been treated by the duke Mou.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: Mencius took his leave of Qi before passing the night in Zhou.

l: Zhou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: Zhou was the place where Mencius spent the night after leaving Qi.

l: visitor (person who wished to detain Mencius), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: The visitor came to speak with Mencius on behalf of the king and was displeased when Mencius slept instead of listening. He later heard Mencius explain that his plans did not treat Mencius as Zi Si had been treated.

l: duke Mou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: The duke Mou retained Zi Si by keeping a person beside him. He also needed a remembrancer beside him in order to make Xie Liu and Shen Xiang feel at home and remain with him.

l: Zi Si, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: Zi Si would not have remained with the duke Mou if the duke had not kept a person by his side.

l: detaining Mencius on behalf of the king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: The visitor wished to detain Mencius on behalf of the king and approached him to discuss the matter.

l: plans concerning Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 11
s: The visitor anxiously formed plans concerning Mencius, but Mencius said that the visitor did not treat him as the duke Mou had treated Zi Si.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: Yin Shi criticizes Mencius for leaving Qi after failing to find a suitable ruler and for delaying his departure from Zhou. Mencius explains that he wanted to serve the king, hoped the king would change, and felt constrained to leave when the king did not recall him. He says that using him would benefit the people of the whole kingdom, not only Qi, and contrasts his conduct with that of small-minded remonstrants. Yin Shi accepts the explanation and admits that he is a small man.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: Mencius leaves Qi after not finding in the king a ruler to suit him, but says he did not desire to leave and hoped the king would change and recall him. He maintains that serving the king could bring happiness to the people of the whole kingdom, and he distinguishes his conduct from that of small-minded people who leave in anger after their remonstrances are rejected.

l: Yin Shi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: Yin Shi criticizes Mencius's intelligence, motives, and delayed departure from Zhou. After hearing Mencius's explanation, Yin Shi admits that he is a small man.

l: king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: The king of Qi does not send after Mencius when Mencius leaves Zhou. Mencius believes the king may still be made to do what is good and hopes that the king will change and use him.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: Mencius says that if the king used him, the resulting happiness would extend beyond the people of Qi to the people of the whole kingdom.

l: Mencius's departure from office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: Mencius's departure from Qi follows his failure to find in the king a ruler to suit him, but he says he was constrained to leave rather than acting from personal desire. He stopped three nights before leaving Zhou because he still hoped the king would change and recall him.

l: the king's change of mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 12
s: Mencius continues to hope daily that the king will change. He says that if the king had changed, he would certainly have recalled him.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: Mencius left Qi, and Chong Yu questioned him about his dissatisfied appearance. Mencius explained that the expected time for a true royal sovereign and illustrious individuals had arrived, but Heaven did not yet wish the kingdom to have tranquillity and good order. He said that if Heaven wished for this, he was the one who could bring it about, which explained his dissatisfaction.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: Mencius left Qi. When Chong Yu questioned his dissatisfied appearance, Mencius explained that the expected time for a true royal sovereign had arrived and that he could bring tranquillity and good order to the kingdom if Heaven wished it.

l: Chong Yu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: Chong Yu questioned Mencius on the way after Mencius left Qi, asking about his dissatisfied appearance and recalling Mencius's teaching that the superior man does not murmur against Heaven or grudge against men.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: Qi was left by Mencius.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: Heaven did not yet wish the kingdom to enjoy tranquillity and good order. Mencius said that if Heaven wished this, he could bring it about.

l: the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: The kingdom did not yet enjoy tranquillity and good order because Heaven did not yet wish it to do so.

l: tranquillity and good order, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 13
s: Tranquillity and good order were described as the condition Heaven might wish the kingdom to enjoy, and Mencius said he could bring them about if Heaven wished.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Mencius left Qi and dwelt in Xiu. In response to Gong Sun Chou, Mencius explained that the ancients did not generally hold office without receiving salary. Mencius had intended to leave after seeing the king in Chong and therefore declined salary, but orders for the collection of troops made it improper to ask permission to leave, although remaining in Qi was not his purpose.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Mencius left Qi and dwelt in Xiu. He intended to leave after seeing the king in Chong, declined to receive salary, and later remained because orders for the collection of troops made it improper to ask permission to leave.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Qi was the place Mencius left and had previously entered. Mencius remained there longer than he intended.

l: Xiu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Xiu was the place where Mencius dwelt after leaving Qi.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Gong Sun Chou asked Mencius whether the ancients held office without receiving salary.

l: salary, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Salary was declined by Mencius because he intended to leave after his interview with the king in Chong. He explained that the ancients did not generally hold office without receiving it.

l: king (in Chong), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: The king in Chong was seen by Mencius during an interview before Mencius intended to leave.

l: Chong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Chong was the place where Mencius saw the king.

l: orders for the collection of troops, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 14
s: Orders for the collection of troops arrived after Mencius declined salary. Their arrival made it improper for him to beg permission to leave.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: The prince, afterwards duke Wen of Teng, visits Mencius while traveling to Chu by way of Song and hears that human nature is good, with Yao and Shun praised. On his return from Chu, he visits Mencius again and is urged not to doubt that the path to excellence is one and available to everyone. Mencius cites Cheng Gan, Yan Yuan, Gong Ming Yi, King Wen, and the duke of Zhou to support this teaching. Mencius says Teng is small but sufficient to become a good State and compares his instruction to medicine that must provoke a commotion to cure disease.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Mencius receives the prince, afterwards duke Wen of Teng, during his journeys to and from Chu. He teaches that human nature is good, praises Yao and Shun, urges the prince not to doubt his words, and says that Teng is sufficient to become a good State.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Before becoming duke Wen of Teng, the prince visits Mencius while traveling to Chu by way of Song and visits him again on the return journey. He hears Mencius explain that human excellence is attainable and that Teng, though small, can become a good State.

l: Chu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Chu is the destination to which the prince, afterwards duke Wen of Teng, travels. The prince visits Mencius on the way to Chu and again while returning from it.

l: Song, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Song is the place through which the prince, afterwards duke Wen of Teng, travels on his way to Chu. He visits Mencius there.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Teng is described by Mencius as small, amounting to about fifty li in length and breadth, but still sufficient to make a good State. Mencius encourages its ruler to pursue the one path to excellence.

l: human nature, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Mencius teaches the prince, afterwards duke Wen of Teng, that human nature is good.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Shun is praised by Mencius as an example of human excellence. Yan Yuan is quoted as asking what kind of man Shun was and asserting that one who exerts himself can also become such as Shun was.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: After Duke Ding of Teng dies, the prince sends Ran You to consult Mencius about funeral duties. Mencius teaches that the three years’ mourning and related practices were prescribed by the three dynasties for everyone from the sovereign to the common people. Although the prince’s aged relatives and officers oppose the practice, Mencius says the prince must set the example himself. The prince observes mourning, and the interment draws people from across the State, who are impressed by his grief.

l: the prince (successor to Duke Ding of Teng), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: After Duke Ding of Teng dies, the prince asks Ran You to consult Mencius about the funeral duties. He decides to observe three years’ mourning despite opposition, then lives in the shed for five months without issuing orders or cautions and sets an example of deep grief at the interment.

l: Ran You, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Ran You goes to Zou twice to consult Mencius for the prince. He reports Mencius’s advice and commission back to the prince.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Mencius advises that men should do their utmost in discharging funeral duties to parents. He teaches that three years’ mourning and related practices were prescribed by the three dynasties, and later says that the prince must seek the remedy in himself and set the example for his inferiors.

l: Zou, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Zou is the place to which Ran You travels to consult Mencius.

l: the prince's aged relatives, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: The prince’s aged relatives oppose his decision to observe three years’ mourning. Later, they say that the prince may be understood to know the ceremonies after he has dwelt in the shed for five months.

l: the officers, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: The officers oppose the prince’s observance of three years’ mourning, arguing that former princes did not follow the practice. Later, they say that the prince may be understood to know the ceremonies.

l: funeral duties, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that in discharging funeral duties to parents, men should do their utmost. The prince seeks advice about the various services connected with these duties.

l: three years' mourning, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that three years’ mourning, along with the coarse garment and eating of congee, was prescribed by the three dynasties and binding on all. The prince determines to observe it despite opposition.

l: the ceremonies, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says he has not learned the ceremonies observed by princes, but identifies several mourning practices as prescribed by the three dynasties. The prince’s aged relatives and officers later judge that he understands the ceremonies.

l: the death of Duke Ding of Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: The death of Duke Ding of Teng causes the great duty of mourning and funeral observance to devolve upon his successor, the prince.

l: the interment, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: At the time of interment, people come from all quarters of the State to witness it. Visitors from other States who come to condole are greatly pleased by the prince’s deep dejection and mournful wailing and weeping.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius about governing, and Mencius explains that the people need a secure livelihood, fair land arrangements, and education. Mencius contrasts the tax system with the system of mutual aid, arguing that taxation can burden the people in bad years. He urges the establishment of educational institutions and says Teng can renew its kingdom through benevolent government. Mencius later explains the nine-squares system of dividing the land to Bi Zhan, including the cultivation of a public field by eight families.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius about the proper way of governing a kingdom. He chooses Bi Zhan to consult Mencius about the nine-squares system of dividing the land.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Mencius teaches that the people must have a secure livelihood, fair land arrangements, and education. He explains the systems of taxation and mutual aid, advises the establishment of educational institutions, and describes how Teng may apply the nine-squares system.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Teng is described as a narrow and small territory that nevertheless contains both men of a superior grade and country-men. Mencius says its boundaries should be correctly defined and its land and allowances regulated according to a system of mutual aid and adjusted by the prince and his officials.

l: the people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: The people lack a fixed heart when they lack a secure livelihood, making them vulnerable to self-abandonment, moral deflection, depravity, and wild license. They should receive fair treatment, education, mutual assistance, and protection from oppressive exactions.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Benevolent government begins by securing the people's livelihood and correctly defining land boundaries. Mencius presents it as involving fair land division, regulated allowances, education, and mutual aid.

l: tax system, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: The tax system fixes the regular amount by averaging several years. It may seem light in good years but can require the full amount in bad years, leaving the people unable to nourish their parents and forcing them to borrow.

l: system of mutual aid, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: The system of mutual aid involves mutual dependence and a public field cultivated by families who also work their private fields. Mencius recommends reserving one division for it in the remoter districts of Teng.

l: nine-squares system of dividing the land, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: The nine-squares system divides a square li into nine squares containing nine hundred mu. The central square is public, while eight families each receive a private hundred mu and cultivate the public field together before attending to their private affairs.

l: public field, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: The public field is the central square in the nine-squares system. Eight families cultivate it in common, and they must finish the public work before turning to their private affairs.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 concerns Xu Xing's teachings and Mencius's responses to them. Xu Xing teaches that rulers should cultivate the ground and work alongside their people, while Mencius argues for the division of labor and the distinct duties of rulers, husbandmen, and handicraftsmen. Mencius also recounts how Yao, Shun, Yu, and other sages secured food, order, and moral instruction for the people. The chapter concludes with Mencius rejecting Xu Xing's claim that equal prices would eliminate deceit in the market.

l: Chapter 4, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 presents Xu Xing's doctrines and Mencius's arguments against them, including discussions of labor, government, ancient sages, moral instruction, and market prices.

l: Xu Xing, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Xu Xing comes from Chu to Teng and claims to act according to the words of Shen Nong. He teaches that wise rulers should cultivate the ground, prepare their own meals, and govern alongside their people.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Duke Wen gives Xu Xing a dwelling-place after Xu Xing asks to become one of his people.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Teng receives Xu Xing and his disciples, and its prince is praised as a worthy ruler who practices benevolent government.

l: Chen Xiang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Chen Xiang comes from Song with his younger brother and becomes greatly pleased with Xu Xing, abandoning what he had learned to become Xu Xing's disciple. He reports and defends Xu Xing's teachings in conversation with Mencius.

l: Chen Liang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Chen Liang is identified as Chen Xiang's teacher and as a native of Chu who studied the doctrines of Zhou Gong and Zhong Ni in the Middle Kingdom.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Mencius questions Chen Xiang about Xu Xing's practices and argues that exchange, specialized work, and government cannot be rejected in favor of universal self-sufficiency. He also recounts the work of ancient sages and rejects Xu Xing's market doctrine.

l: Xu Xing's doctrines, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Xu Xing's doctrines hold that princes should farm and prepare their own food with their people. They also claim that equal standards and prices for goods would prevent deceit in the kingdom.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Benevolent government is associated with the prince of Teng, whose rule attracts Xu Xing and others. Mencius presents governing, teaching, and benefiting the people as responsibilities of those who rule.

l: handicraftsmen, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Handicraftsmen produce articles such as caps, boilers, pans, and iron shares, which are exchanged for grain. Mencius says their work cannot be carried on together with the work of husbandry by the same individual.

l: division of labor, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Division of labor is expressed through the principle that some labor with their minds and govern others, while some labor with their strength and are governed by others. Those who are governed support those who govern, and those who govern are supported by them.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Yao suffers anxiety over the disorder caused by floods, vegetation, and beasts, and raises Shun to office. His concern is said to be finding Shun rather than cultivating his own hundred mu.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Shun directs measures to regulate the disorder and appoints Xie to teach the relations of humanity. His anxiety is described as finding Yu and Gao Yao.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Yu separates and regulates waterways, leading them to the sea or the Jiang. He is away from home for eight years and passes his door three times without entering.

l: moral nature, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Mencius says that men possess a moral nature, but that people who are well fed, clothed, and housed without instruction become almost like beasts.

l: relations of humanity, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The relations of humanity are taught as affection between father and son, righteousness between sovereign and minister, separate functions between husband and wife, order between old and young, and fidelity between friends.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Confucius is quoted as praising the greatness of Yao and the majesty of Shun, saying that Yao corresponded to Heaven and that Shun possessed the kingdom while seeming to regard it as nothing.

l: the kingdom, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The kingdom requires government, moral instruction, and the work of different occupations. Mencius says that reducing all goods to one standard would throw the kingdom into confusion.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Benevolence is described as finding a person who will benefit the kingdom. Mencius says that giving the throne to another person is easy, while finding such a beneficial person is difficult.

l: the barbarians of the west and the north, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Mencius says he has heard of people using the doctrines of the great land to change barbarians, but not of barbarians changing others. He calls Xu Xing a shrike-tongued barbarian of the south whose doctrines differ from those of the ancient kings.

l: the Middle Kingdom, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The Middle Kingdom is where Yu's flood-control work makes cultivation possible and where Chen Liang studies the doctrines of Zhou Gong and Zhong Ni.

l: Zhou Gong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Zhou Gong's doctrines are among those studied by Chen Liang. Mencius cites the Praise-songs of Lu as saying that Zhou Gong smote the barbarians of the west and north and punished Jing and Shu.

l: Zhong Ni, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Zhong Ni's doctrines are studied by Chen Liang together with those of Zhou Gong in the Middle Kingdom.

l: market, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The market is presented as a place where goods of unequal quality and value are exchanged. Mencius says that making unlike goods equal in price would create confusion and encourage deceit.

l: Xu Xing's market doctrine, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Xu Xing's market doctrine claims that equal quantities, lengths, weights, or sizes of goods should have equal prices, so that no one could impose on another. Mencius rejects it because goods naturally differ in value and equal pricing would discourage the making of larger or better goods.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Yi Zhi, a Mohist, sought to meet Mencius through Xu Bi, and Mencius initially declined because he was unwell. When Mencius agreed to receive him, he criticized Yi Zhi for promoting spare simplicity in funerals while burying his own parents sumptuously. Yi Zhi defended loving all people while beginning with one's parents, but Mencius argued that Heaven gives creatures one root and that filial feeling naturally leads to proper burial. After hearing Mencius's explanation, Yi Zhi acknowledged that Mencius had instructed him.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Mencius first declined to see Yi Zhi because he was unwell, then agreed to meet him so that he could correct Yi Zhi's errors. He argued that affection begins with one's parents and that proper burial follows from natural filial emotion.

l: Yi Zhi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Yi Zhi sought to see Mencius and defended the principle that love should extend to all, while its expression begins with one's parents. Although he supported spare funeral practices, he had buried his own parents sumptuously; after Mencius's explanation, he said that Mencius had instructed him.

l: Xu Bi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Xu Bi served as the intermediary through whom Yi Zhi initially sought to see Mencius.

l: Mohists, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: The Mohists are associated in the discussion with the view that funeral arrangements should follow spare simplicity.

l: Mohist doctrines, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Mohist doctrines are described as teaching spare simplicity in funeral matters and as being used by Yi Zhi to seek changes in the customs of the kingdom.

l: the parents, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: The parents are the immediate object of filial affection and are to be treated with proper burial. Mencius presents the impulse to cover and inter the bodies of deceased parents as arising from natural emotional response.

l: burial of parents, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Burial of parents is discussed as a practice that should follow a proper rule rather than spare simplicity alone. Yi Zhi's sumptuous burial of his parents conflicted with the Mohist view he supported, while Mencius defended handsome burial as consistent with filial virtue.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Part II / Chapter 1
s: Chen Dai questions Mencius's refusal to wait upon the princes, arguing that doing so might enable one of them to become sovereign or chief. Mencius cites Confucius's approval of a forester who refused an inappropriate summons and tells the story of Wang Liang, who declined to drive deceitfully for a mean archer. He argues that bending one's principles for gain is wrong, concluding that no one who bends himself can make others straight.

l: Chen Dai, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Part II / Chapter 1
s: Chen Dai tells Mencius that refusing to wait upon the princes seems like standing on a small point. He argues that waiting upon them might allow one to become sovereign or chief of the other princes.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Part II / Chapter 1
s: Mencius defends his refusal to go to the princes without being invited. He cites Confucius, the conduct of a forester, and Wang Liang's refusal to drive deceitfully to argue that he should not bend his principles for gain.

l: princes, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Part II / Chapter 1
s: The princes are those whom Mencius refuses to wait upon without an invitation. Chen Dai suggests that waiting upon them could enable one of them to become sovereign or chief of the other princes.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Part II / Chapter 1
s: Confucius approves of a determined officer who does not forget possible death and a brave officer who does not forget that he may lose his head. He specifically approves the forester for refusing to go to the duke when summoned by an inappropriate article.

l: principles, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Part II / Chapter 1
s: Mencius says that bending his principles to follow the princes would be improper. He concludes that no one who has bent himself has ever been able to make others straight.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Jing Chun asks Mencius whether Gong Sun Yan and Zhang Yi are great men because their anger frightens the princes and their quietness extinguishes trouble. Mencius rejects this view and contrasts such compliance with the rule for women. He says a great man lives in the wide house, stands in the correct seat, walks in the great path, serves the people when in office, and maintains his principles when disappointed. A great man is not swayed by riches, poverty, or power.

l: Jing Chun, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Jing Chun asks Mencius whether Gong Sun Yan and Zhang Yi are really great men. He describes their anger as frightening all the princes and their quietness as extinguishing trouble throughout the kingdom.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Mencius rejects Jing Chun's claim that Gong Sun Yan and Zhang Yi are great men. He explains that a great man maintains his principles, serves the people when in office, and remains steady despite riches, poverty, or power.

l: Gong Sun Yan, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Gong Sun Yan is presented by Jing Chun as a man whose anger makes all the princes afraid. He is included with Zhang Yi among those whom Mencius says are not great men.

l: Zhang Yi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Zhang Yi is presented by Jing Chun as a man whose anger makes all the princes afraid. He is included with Gong Sun Yan among those whom Mencius says are not great men.

l: women, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: Women are described through the Ritual Usages as being taught that compliance is their correct course. A young woman is cautioned to be respectful, careful, and obedient to her husband.

l: world, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: The world is described as having a wide house, a correct seat, and a great path. A great man dwells in the wide house, stands in the correct seat, and walks in the great path of the world.

l: the mass of the people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: A great man practices his principles for the good of the people when he obtains his desire for office.

l: great man, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 2
s: A great man dwells in the wide house of the world, stands in its correct seat, and walks in its great path. He practices his principles for the good of the people in office and alone when disappointed, and he is not swayed by riches, poverty, or power.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Zhou Xiao asks Mencius whether superior men of old time took office and why they were so concerned about employment by a ruler. Mencius explains that officers were condoled with after three months without office because losing office is like a prince losing his State, and an officer needs office to fulfill his proper work. He compares an officer carrying his gift of introduction between States to a husbandman carrying his plough. Mencius says that although the ancients desired office, they hated obtaining it through improper means.

l: Zhou Xiao, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Zhou Xiao asks Mencius whether superior men of old time took office. He questions whether condoling with an officer after three months of unemployment showed excessive urgency and asks why a superior man might make difficulty about taking office.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Mencius says that superior men of old time took office and that officers unemployed for three months were condoled with. He explains that losing office is like a prince losing his State, compares office to a husbandman's plough, and says the ancients desired office but rejected improper ways of obtaining it.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Confucius is described as looking anxious and unhappy after three months without employment by a ruler. When he passed from the boundary of a State, he carried his proper gift of introduction with him.

l: officers, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Officers were condoled with when they had been unemployed by a ruler for three months. Their loss of office is compared to a prince's loss of his State, and their office is compared to a husbandman's plough that is carried from one State to another.

l: office, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Office is presented as necessary for an officer's proper work, like a plough is necessary for a husbandman. The ancients desired office but did not accept obtaining it by an improper way.

l: seeking office by an improper way, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 3
s: Seeking office by an improper way is compared to young people boring holes to steal a sight of each other or getting over a wall to be together. The ancients desired office but hated obtaining it in this manner.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Peng Geng questions Mencius about whether it is extravagant for a scholar to move between princes and receive substantial support without performing ordinary labor. Mencius argues that support is proper when there is a proper ground for receiving it, comparing the scholar’s service to the interdependence of farmers, textile workers, carpenters, and carriage-wrights. He maintains that a scholar who is filial, respectful, and preserves benevolence and righteousness serves society and deserves support. Mencius concludes that people remunerate work done rather than intention, as shown by refusing to pay someone who damages tiles and walls.

l: Peng Geng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Peng Geng asks Mencius whether it is extravagant for a scholar to live upon different princes while accompanied by many carriages and attendants. He argues that supporting a scholar who performs no ordinary service is improper, but accepts that remuneration is based on work done rather than intention.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Mencius argues that receiving support is not excessive when there is a proper ground for it. He says that a scholar who is filial, respectful, and preserves the principles of the ancient kings serves others through benevolence and righteousness and deserves support.

l: scholar, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The scholar is described as moving between princes and receiving support despite performing no ordinary trade. A scholar who is filial at home, respectful abroad, and watches over ancient principles is presented as providing a service worthy of support.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The superior man practices principles, but Mencius says his purpose in doing so is not the relevant issue. His service to others makes him deserving of support.

l: carpenters, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Carpenters are presented as workers whose trade enables them to obtain food from others through the interchange of labor and services.

l: carriage-wrights, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Carriage-wrights are presented as workers whose trade enables them to obtain food from others. Peng Geng initially contrasts their trade with the superior man's practice of principles.

l: intercommunication of the productions of labour, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The intercommunication of the productions of labour allows people to exchange the products of their work. Without it, husbandmen and women would each have a superfluity of their own products.

l: interchange of men's services, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: The interchange of men's services allows one person's overplus to supply another person's deficiency. Through it, workers such as carpenters and carriage-wrights can receive food from others.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Benevolence and righteousness are the principles practiced by the scholar who is filial, respectful, and preserves the teachings of the ancient kings. Mencius treats this practice as a service that merits support.

l: support, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Support should be given when there is a proper ground for receiving it. Mencius argues that a scholar who serves society through virtuous conduct deserves support, just as workers receive support through exchanged labor.

l: service, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 4
s: Service, rather than intention, is what Mencius says should be remunerated. The example of a person who damages tiles and walls shows that an intention to earn a living does not justify payment without useful work done.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Wan Zhang asks Mencius what Song should do because Qi and Chu attack its ruler, who is said to be practising true royal government. Mencius recounts how Tang punished the chief of Ge after his people robbed and killed provision-carriers, and how Tang’s campaigns won popular support. He also describes how king Wu rescued the people of Shang by destroying their oppressors. Mencius concludes that if Song truly practised royal government, people throughout the four seas would want its ruler as their sovereign, leaving little for Qi and Chu to threaten.

l: Wan Zhang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Wan Zhang asks Mencius what should be done because Song is small and Qi and Chu hate and attack its ruler.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Mencius answers Wan Zhang by recounting Tang’s punishment of Ge and king Wu’s campaign against Shang. He concludes that genuine royal government would attract the people throughout the four seas to Song’s ruler.

l: Song, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Song is described as a small State whose ruler is said to be setting about practising true royal government. Mencius says that if Song were truly practising it, people throughout the four seas would seek its ruler, and Qi and Chu would pose little threat.

l: true royal government, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: True royal government is presented as a rule that wins the longing and support of people throughout the four seas. Mencius says its practice would cause people to look for the ruler as their sovereign.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Qi hates and attacks the ruler of Song. Mencius says that if Song truly practised royal government, Qi would not be much to fear.

l: Chu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Chu hates and attacks the ruler of Song. Mencius says that if Song truly practised royal government, Chu would not be much to fear.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Tang sent aid to the State of Ge when its chief claimed to lack sacrificial victims and millet. After the chief of Ge’s people robbed and killed provision-carriers, Tang punished him, and Tang’s campaigns gained the people’s support.

l: State of Ge, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: The State of Ge adjoined the place where Tang dwelt in Bo. Its chief neglected sacrifices, and Tang later punished the State of Ge after its people attacked provision-carriers.

l: chief of Ge, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: The chief of Ge neglected proper sacrifices and consumed the oxen and sheep Tang sent. He then led his people to rob provisions from Tang’s labourers, and a boy carrying millet and flesh was killed and robbed, leading Tang to punish him.

l: Tang's punishment of Ge, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Tang punished the chief of Ge because of the murder and robbery of a boy carrying food for labourers. The people throughout the four seas said Tang acted to avenge a common man and woman rather than to gain wealth.

l: the four seas, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: All within the four seas supported Tang’s punishment of Ge and longed for Tang like people longing for rain during severe drought. Mencius says that if Song truly practised royal government, all within the four seas would seek its ruler.

l: Tang's punitive expeditions, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Tang made eleven punitive expeditions and had no enemy in the kingdom. As he moved among different regions, people complained that he was making them last, showing their desire for his arrival.

l: people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: The people welcomed Tang’s progress, which is compared to timely rain, while markets and field work continued normally. King Wu also gave tranquillity to the people of Shang, who welcomed him with gifts and joined themselves to Zhou.

l: Zhou dynasty, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Zhou is the dynasty whose sovereign the people of Shang said they would serve in order to be made happy. The men of station of Zhou were met by men of station of Shang bearing black and yellow silks.

l: king Wu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: King Wu proceeded against those who would not become subjects of Zhou and gave tranquillity to their people. He rescued the people of Shang from fire and water by seizing and destroying their oppressors.

l: Wu's campaign against Shang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Wu’s campaign against Shang targeted the oppressors rather than the people. The people welcomed Wu, offered black and yellow silks, rice, and congee, and joined themselves as subjects to Zhou.

l: Shang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: Some people of Shang would not become subjects of Zhou until king Wu proceeded against them. After Wu’s campaign, Shang’s people were given tranquillity and welcomed him, while Shang’s oppressors were seized and destroyed.

l: oppressors, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 5
s: The oppressors of Shang were seized and destroyed by Wu. His campaign is described as saving the people from the midst of fire and water while targeting only those oppressors.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: Mencius tells Dai Bu Sheng how the king of Song may be made virtuous. He explains that a person cannot learn a language if surrounded by people speaking another language, despite repeated punishment. Mencius argues that if all the king’s attendants were Xue Ju Zhous, the king would have no one with whom to do evil, but if none were like Xue Ju Zhou, he would have no one with whom to do good. He concludes that one Xue Ju Zhou cannot accomplish much alone for the king of Song.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: Mencius tells Dai Bu Sheng how the king of Song may be made virtuous. He argues that the king’s attendants, rather than one person alone, determine whether the king has people with whom to do good or evil.

l: Dai Bu Sheng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: Dai Bu Sheng is told by Mencius how the king of Song may be made virtuous. He agrees that a great officer of Chu would employ a man of Qi to teach his son the speech of Qi.

l: king of Song, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: The king of Song is placed in attendance with Xue Ju Zhou, whom Dai Bu Sheng supposes to be a scholar of virtue. Mencius says that one Xue Ju Zhou cannot accomplish much alone for the king.

l: Xue Ju Zhou, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: Xue Ju Zhou is supposed to be a scholar of virtue and is placed in attendance on the king. Mencius says that if all the king’s attendants were Xue Ju Zhous, the king would have no one with whom to do evil.

l: attendants on the king, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: The attendants on the king are described as determining whether the king has people with whom to do good or evil. If they are all Xue Ju Zhous, the king has no one with whom to do evil; if none are Xue Ju Zhous, he has no one with whom to do good.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 6
s: Virtue is associated with Xue Ju Zhou, who is supposed to be a scholar of virtue. Mencius explains that the king’s exposure to virtuous or non-virtuous attendants affects what the king can do.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius about the righteousness involved in not going to see the princes. Mencius explains examples of avoiding or meeting princes, including Duan Gan Mu, Xie Liu, Yang Huo, and Confucius. He concludes that remarks by Zengzi and Zi Lu reveal the spirit that the superior man nourishes.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius what point of righteousness is involved in not going to see the princes.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Mencius explains when it is proper or improper to see a prince, citing examples from the ancients and the conduct of Yang Huo and Confucius.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Righteousness is discussed in relation to whether one should go to see princes and how one maintains proper conduct toward them.

l: not going to see the princes, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Not going to see the princes is examined through examples of avoidance, including Duan Gan Mu and Xie Liu, whose scrupulosity Mencius considers excessive.

l: Yang Huo, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Yang Huo wanted Confucius to visit him but arranged to send a roasted pig while Confucius was away, following the rule concerning gifts from a great officer to a scholar.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: Confucius watched when Yang Huo was away and went to pay his respects after Yang Huo had taken the initiative.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: The superior man is described through the spirit he nourishes, which can be understood by considering the remarks of Zengzi and Zi Lu.

l: spirit which the superior man nourishes, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 7
s: The spirit which the superior man nourishes is identified as something revealed by remarks condemning flattering behavior and insincere dealings.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: Dai Ying Zhi tells Mencius that he cannot immediately levy only a tithe and abolish duties at passes and markets. He proposes lightening the tax and duties until next year, then ending them. Mencius compares this delay to a man who takes his neighbor’s strayed fowls and argues that known unrighteousness should be ended without waiting.

l: Dai Ying Zhi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: Dai Ying Zhi says he cannot immediately levy only a tithe and abolish duties at the passes and in the markets. He proposes lightening the tax and duties until next year, then ending them, and asks Mencius what he thinks.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: Mencius responds to Dai Ying Zhi by comparing delayed reform to a man who appropriates his neighbor’s strayed fowls. He says that when something is known to be unrighteous, it should be ended without delay.

l: tithe, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: The levying of a tithe is presented as a measure Dai Ying Zhi is not able to implement immediately.

l: duties, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: Duties charged at the passes and in the markets are to be lightened until next year and then abolished according to Dai Ying Zhi’s proposal.

l: tax, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: Dai Ying Zhi proposes to lighten the tax until next year and then make an end of it.

l: man who appropriates fowls, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: The man appropriates some of his neighbor’s strayed fowls every day. When told that this is not the way of a good man, he proposes taking only one fowl a month until next year, then ending the practice.

l: strayed fowls, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: The strayed fowls belong to the man’s neighbor and are appropriated by the man in Mencius’s example.

l: appropriation of fowls, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: The appropriation of the neighbor’s strayed fowls is described as a practice that should be ended immediately once its unrighteousness is recognized.

l: unrighteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 8
s: Mencius says that if a person knows something is unrighteous, he should use all despatch to put an end to it rather than wait until next year.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Mencius tells Gong Du that he is compelled to dispute because the world has repeatedly fallen into disorder when sage principles decline. He recounts how Yu controlled the great inundation, how Zhou Gong restored order after the tyrant Zhou, and how Confucius used the Spring and Autumn to condemn rebellious ministers and villainous sons. Mencius opposes Yang Zhu and Mo Di because their doctrines deny the claims of the sovereign or the special affection due to a father. He seeks to rectify men's hearts, defend the doctrines of the former sages, and carry on the work of the three sages.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Mencius tells Gong Du that he is not fond of disputing but is compelled to oppose perverse doctrines. He defends the doctrines of the former sages, seeks to rectify men's hearts, and aims to carry on the work of the three sages.

l: the Middle Kingdom, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: The Middle Kingdom was inundated when the waters flowed out of their channels in the time of Yao. People had no settled place there until Yu reduced the waters to order.

l: the people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: The people suffered when floods, oppressive rulers, gardens, parks, and neglected fields deprived them of places to live, clothing, and food. They rejoiced when Zhou Gong drove away ferocious animals and restored repose.

l: the great inundation, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: The great inundation caused waters to flow wildly through the country, forcing people to live in nests, raised platforms, or caves. Yu dug open obstructed channels and conducted the waters to the sea.

l: the principles that mark sages, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: The principles that mark sages fell into decay after the deaths of Yao and Shun. Their decline accompanied the rise of oppressive sovereigns and disorder.

l: Zhou Gong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Zhou Gong assisted king Wu and destroyed Zhou. He smote Yan, put its sovereign to death after three years, drove Fei Lian to the sea and slew him, extinguished fifty States, and drove away ferocious animals.

l: the Spring and Autumn, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: The Spring and Autumn was completed by Confucius and contains matters proper to the sovereign. Confucius said it would cause men both to know and to condemn him.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Confucius was afraid when the world again fell into decay and principles faded away, so he made the Spring and Autumn. Its judgments struck rebellious ministers and villainous sons with terror.

l: Yang Zhu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Yang Zhu's words filled the country alongside those of Mo Di. Mencius opposes Yang Zhu's doctrine because it does not acknowledge the claims of the sovereign.

l: Mo Di, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Mo Di's words filled the country alongside those of Yang Zhu. Mencius opposes Mo Di's doctrine because it teaches equal love and does not acknowledge the peculiar affection due to a father.

l: Yang's principle, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Yang's principle is described as 'each one for himself.' Mencius says that it does not acknowledge the claims of the sovereign.

l: Mo's principle, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Mo's principle is described as 'to love all equally.' Mencius says that it does not acknowledge the peculiar affection due to a father.

l: the doctrines of the former sages, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Mencius addresses himself to defending the doctrines of the former sages and opposing Yang and Mo. He says that sages who rise again will not change his words.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Mencius warns that if the principles of Confucius are not set forth, perverse doctrines will stop up the path of benevolence and righteousness. When they are stopped up, beasts will be led to devour men and men will devour one another.

l: father-deniers and king-deniers, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: Father-deniers and king-deniers are associated with the doctrines of Mo and Yang, which reject the special affection due to a father or the claims of the sovereign. Mencius says that Zhou Gong would have smitten them.

l: the three sages, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 9
s: The three sages are associated with Yu's control of the waters, Zhou Gong's restoration of order, and Confucius's completion of the Spring and Autumn. Mencius seeks to carry on their work.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Kuang Zhang praises Chen Zhong as a man of true self-denying purity because he endured hunger in Wu Ling and ate worm-eaten plums. Mencius argues that Chen Zhong's standards could only be followed by an earthworm and questions the origins of his house and food. Mencius also recounts that Chen Zhong rejects his brother Dai's wealth and house but accepts food from his wife, showing inconsistency in his principles.

l: Kuang Zhang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Kuang Zhang presents Chen Zhong as a man of true self-denying purity. He points to Chen Zhong's hunger in Wu Ling and his eating of worm-eaten plums as evidence.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Mencius regards Chen Zhong as outstanding among the scholars of Qi but denies that he possesses the self-denying purity he claims. He argues that Chen Zhong's principles would require him to live like an earthworm and criticizes his inconsistent conduct toward his brother's property and his wife's food.

l: Chen Zhong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Chen Zhong lived in Wu Ling and went three days without food until he could neither hear nor see, then recovered after eating three mouthfuls of worm-eaten plums. He rejects his brother Dai's emolument and house as unrighteous, yet eats food given by his wife and lives in Wu Ling.

l: Wu Ling, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Wu Ling is where Chen Zhong lived after avoiding his brother and leaving his mother. Chen Zhong later returned to his family's house for a time.

l: self-denying purity, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Self-denying purity is the quality Kuang Zhang attributes to Chen Zhong. Mencius says Chen Zhong does not truly possess it because his conduct is inconsistent.

l: earthworm, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: An earthworm eats dry mould above and drinks the yellow spring below. Mencius says that only by becoming an earthworm could a person fully carry out the principles Chen Zhong holds.

l: Dai, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: Dai is Chen Zhong's elder brother and received a revenue of 10,000 zhong from Gai. Chen Zhong considered Dai's emolument and house unrighteous and refused to eat of the former or dwell in the latter.

l: principles held by Chen Zhong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), Chapter 10
s: The principles held by Chen Zhong require rejecting property and food considered unrighteous. Mencius says they could only be consistently carried out by an earthworm and points to Chen Zhong's acceptance of his wife's food as an inconsistency.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Mencius explains that skill, virtue, and benevolent intentions cannot govern effectively without instruments, laws, and the practices of the ancient kings. He argues that benevolent government brings order and benefits to the people, while rulers and ministers who disregard principle, laws, propriety, and righteousness spread disorder through the kingdom. The text warns that a State is ruined not mainly by weak defenses or poor resources, but when superiors violate propriety and inferiors fail to learn. It also teaches that serving a sovereign properly requires urging difficult achievements, promoting good, and restraining perversity.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Mencius teaches that virtue alone is insufficient for government and that laws require proper implementation. He argues that only the benevolent should occupy high stations and that officials should respectfully urge their sovereign toward difficult achievements, good conduct, and the suppression of perversity.

l: princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Princes may possess benevolent hearts and a reputation for benevolence while providing no benefits to the people or example for future ages if they do not practice the ways of the ancient kings.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: The people receive no benefits when princes merely possess benevolent intentions without putting the ways of the ancient kings into practice. They suffer when wickedness is disseminated from high stations.

l: ancient kings, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: The ancient kings established ways and laws that should be followed in government. Following their laws is presented as a path by which no one falls into error.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: A kingdom is not made safe merely by complete walls, abundant weapons, extended cultivable land, or accumulated stores and wealth. It faces calamity when superiors violate righteousness and inferiors violate penal laws, and it perishes when propriety is not observed and learned.
